props.title: Rififi
props.initialSlug: Meticulous thieves plan the perfect jewel heist

sections.content: Rififi (1955) revolutionized the heist film genre with its legendary 30-minute silent robbery sequence - a masterclass in sustained tension without dialogue or music. Director Jules Dassin, blacklisted from Hollywood, crafted this French noir after fleeing to Europe, bringing hard-boiled American sensibilities to the Paris underworld. The film's influence echoes through classics like Ocean's Eleven (1960), The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974), and Heat (1995). Its meticulous attention to criminal technique was so detailed that real thieves allegedly used it as a tutorial, leading to its ban in several countries.

sections.content: The French crime film tradition that Rififi helped establish reached its apex with Jean-Pierre Melville's cool, methodical thrillers of the 1960s and 70s. Le Samouraï (1967) and Le Cercle Rouge (1970) refined the genre's focus on professional criminals with rigid codes of honor, while expanding its visual vocabulary of rain-slicked streets, fedoras, and trench coats. This distinctly French take on crime cinema influenced American directors like Michael Mann, whose Thief (1981) and Heat (1995) share Rififi's emphasis on procedure and professionalism. SUBHEAD: The Art of the Silent Heist Sequence

Rififi's wordless robbery scene created a template that countless films have followed. Mission: Impossible (1996) echoed it with its CIA vault break-in, while The Silent Partner (1978) and Drive (2011) borrowed its nerve-wracking combination of precision and impending doom. Even Army of Thieves (2021) directly references Rififi's techniques. The sequence works because it respects both the technical complexity of the heist and the human drama of four men working in desperate silence.
